source.title: Blended Intelligence: A Framework for How Professionally Diverse Multi-disciplinary Teams Solve Problems in Elite Sport

paper.citation: King R. Blended Intelligence: A Framework for How Professionally Diverse Multi-disciplinary Teams Solve Problems in Elite Sport. Lancashire Online Knowledge - University of Lancashire. 2026. doi:10.17030/UCLAN.THESIS.00058103.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How do individual practitioners, multidisciplinary teams, and high-performance leaders conceptualize and execute problem solving? High-performance sport practitioners and leaders from multiple professional disciplines. Performance-related practitioners were overrepresented. Pragmatic mixed qualitative design. Used Likert surveys, heat-map visualization, focus groups, and semistructured interviews.
paper.tldr: The thesis proposes “blended intelligence” as combining deep specialist expertise with collaborative problem-solving capability. Practice implications emphasize structured collaboration, cognitive flexibility, shared language, and leadership conditions that allow expertise to integrate. Use blended intelligence as an operating design: define the problem before assigning disciplines, make assumptions visible, select the expertise the problem needs, and document how the team reached and will revisit its decision.
paper.methods: Pragmatic mixed qualitative design. Used Likert surveys, heat-map visualization, focus groups, and semistructured interviews. Reflexive thematic analysis supported an inductive, researcher-involved interpretation.
paper.findings: The thesis proposes “blended intelligence” as combining deep specialist expertise with collaborative problem-solving capability. Practice implications emphasize structured collaboration, cognitive flexibility, shared language, and leadership conditions that allow expertise to integrate. Blending perspectives is presented as most valuable for ill-defined problems that cannot be solved within one discipline.
paper.limitations: The sample skewed toward performance practitioners and did not specifically analyze gender representation. Likert responses may be vulnerable to acquiescence and rapid-completion bias. Reflexive thematic analysis produces a situated interpretation rather than a universal team model. The framework has not yet demonstrated better athlete outcomes than alternative MDT structures.
paper.practicalImplications: Use blended intelligence as an operating design: define the problem before assigning disciplines, make assumptions visible, select the expertise the problem needs, and document how the team reached and will revisit its decision.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, use blended intelligence as an operating design: define the problem before assigning disciplines, make assumptions visible, select the expertise the problem needs, and document how the team reached and will revisit its decision. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: The paper did not validate a rehabilitation or return-to-sport decision rule. Its findings may inform supporting training or monitoring during reconditioning, but it provides no standalone clearance threshold or progression criterion.
